Title: Top Boy series 3 review — brilliant, bruising drama comes to an end on Netflix
Netflix doesn’t have a single live sports streaming deal, but it’s dominating the sports game
Text: [Netflix has built a multi-billion dollar streaming business by keeping viewers hooked with cliffhangers and unexpected plot twists. Now, the company is hoping it can carry out an offscreen surprise in its own business as its competitors pile into live sports programming.Streaming companies like Apple, Google-owned YouTube and Amazon are all betting big on sports. Apple is paying $250 million per year to show every Major League Soccer match for 10 years (CEO Tim Cook name-checked soccer superstar Lionel Messi three times in the company’s most recent earnings call). And NFL rights are reportedly costing Amazon and YouTube a respective $1 billion and $2 billion annually.Netflix—the platform with the highest number of subscribers at 238 million—appears to be stuck on the sidelines. In November, it will host its first ever live sporting event: a celebrity golf tournament. It’s a far cry from the razzle dazzle of Monday Night Football.But Netflix’s sports strategy is not as lackluster as it might seem. The company is taking a different approach to cash in on viewer demand for sports programming. Instead of plunking down huge sums of money for broadcast rights to games—something that co-CEO Ted Sarandos has said Netflix hasn’t found a way to do profitably—Netflix is using its strength in storytelling to create a deep catalog of docu-series about various sports and athletes.Netflix users might recognize the slew of sports content that has materialized on their home pages in recent years, much of which adheres to a similar format: A camera crew follows a set of athletes through their season for a behind-the-scenes look at their wins, losses and personal lives. The first for Netflix was Formula 1: Drive to Survive, a five-season show following race car drivers, managers and team owners. Netflix has expanded its unofficial genre to include Break Point about tennis stars, Full Swing for golf, Quarterback, Cheer, Tour de France: Unchained and more. It isn’t slowing down. Earlier this month, the company announced it is developing a series following track and field athletes.Story continuesThis strategy lets Netflix reach the same sports-loving audience without having to pay the steep price of showing live sports, says Dan Rayburn, an independent streaming industry analyst and consultant. He reckons the cost of sports documentaries is also significantly lower than the fictional scripted series that Netflix produces.And unlike live sporting events, a highly perishable form of content, documentaries about athletes and sports can retain their appeal with viewers for a longer period of time.It is difficult to determine how profitable these sports docu-series are for Netflix, because it doesn’t release figures for the genre. “But if it wasn’t working, they wouldn’t keep making more,” Rayburn told Fortune. Why sports leagues love docu-seriesThe idea isn’t totally novel. HBO, part of streaming service Max, premiered Hard Knocks in 2001. The series follows NFL teams through training camp, and it is still on air. Hard Knocks was a reference point for the team that created Netflix’s Drive to Survive on what the show should look and feel like, according to Paul Martin, co-founder of Box to Box Films, which produced the racing docu-series. Drive to Survive routinely sits on Netflix’s Top 10 Most Watched list when new seasons come out, with more than 6.8 million people having tuned into the show, according to YouGov Sports, a sports research company. Nielsen credits the show for creating a 2.3% increase in Formula 1 auto-racing viewership, as part of a larger 10% bump since 2019. Formula 1 was also able to sell its broadcasting rights to ESPN in 2022 for more than $75 million per year, skyrocketing from the previous $5 million they were worth, according to the Sports Business Journal.“After the success of Drive to Survive, sports leagues looked around and realized they could do that kind of show and have a similar effect on their sport,” Martin told Fortune. Along with Drive to Survive, Martin produced Break Point, Full Swing and Tour de France: Unchained. He is also producing the new docu-series about runners for Netflix.In other words, Netflix is tapping into the interest in individual sports and driving up the value of the sporting events, without shouldering the cost of the increased demand.WASHINGTON, DC - JULY 19: Mikel Arteta, Bradley Wright-Phillips, and Sacha Kljestan on Apple TV before a game between Arsenal and Major League Soccer at Audi Field on July 19, 2023 in Washington, DC. (Photo by Stephen Nadler/ISI Photos/Getty Images)Live sports bring huge audiences, with 58 million Americans watching sporting events at least once per month, according to the most recent data from Statista in 2021. But it can be difficult to make money broadcasting live games. The rights are expensive, and negotiations are difficult and time-consuming. Amazon reportedly lost “hundreds of millions” of dollars its first year streaming Thursday Night Football, according to The Information. For YouTube, experts expect the Sunday Ticket will act as a loss leader. DirecTV, which formerly owned the rights, was reportedly losing $500 million on the package annually.By sitting out of the live sports competition, Netflix also avoids the costs and logistical challenges of broadcasting live, including hiring camera crews and announcers. Netflix had technical trouble in April when the tech behind its live Love Is Blind reunion failed—if something like that happened during the final minutes of a big game, the damage to the Netflix brand could be massive.Better than a true crime seriesWhile some sports docu-series with this all-access style have found homes on other streaming platforms—like Make or Break about professional surfers on Apple TV+—it’s noteworthy that most have ended up on Netflix.“The tennis guys were set in wanting to be with Netflix because of the reach and audience,” Martin said about producing Break Point. The idea for the show started with him and the Association of Tennis Professionals, the governing body of men’s tennis. They then brought in the Women’s Tennis Association and pitched the series to Netflix, he said.For the upcoming track and field series, the idea came from a lunch with Netflix where someone said, “Why don’t we just do the 100 meters?” according to Martin. Everyone thought it was a great idea, and Netflix brought in World Athletics, the professional association behind the sport, he said.“Everyone in the sports world understands there’s an appetite for these shows,” Martin said. It makes sense for Netflix to stay with this model rather than purchasing the rights to the sports games. Netflix isn’t in the business of creating value in something and then having to pay larger prices for rights, he said.As for the future of the genre, consumers can expect to see more streaming companies shift their budgets to produce live sports docu-series, according to Rayburn, the streaming analyst. Companies are always moving money towards what’s hot, from police procedurals to reality dating series to true crime. And right now, he said, people are talking about the style of sports documentaries Netflix has its money on.This story was originally featured on Fortune.comMore from Fortune: 5 side hustles where you may earn over $20,000 per year—all while working from homeWant more for your money? Title: Pinochet becomes a vampire in Chilean director Larrain's Venice entry 'El Conde'
Text: [By Hanna RantalaVENICE, Aug 31 (Reuters) - Chilean director Pablo Larrain, known for his Jackie Kennedy and Princess Diana dramas "Jackie" and "Spencer," chose General Augusto Pinochet as the subject of his latest film, "El Conde".The movie, which is screening in competition at the Venice Film Festival, depicts Pinochet as a 250-year-old vampire whose family gathers at his remote hideout as he decides his time on earth has come to an end.As Chile prepares to mark the 50th anniversary of the 1973 coup that brought Pinochet to power, Larrain said it was time to show him on the screen."Pinochet has never been filmed before, never been portrayed, whether in cinema or television," Larrain told a Venice press conference ahead of the Netflix title's premiere.The filmmaker, who co-wrote the movie's screenplay, chose to tell the dictator's story as a gruesome black-and-white satire."Probably it's the only way. I think that if you were to avoid the satire, it could easily take you towards some form of empathy (towards Pinochet), and that's not acceptable," said Larrain.During Pinochet's bloody 17-year dictatorship, 1,469 people were forcibly disappeared, and thousands more tortured as political prisoners, according to the Ministry of Justice, based on fact-finding by various commissions.Pinochet, who died in December 2006 at the age of 91, was never convicted of his responsibility for the crimes."There is a resurgence of the extreme right in Chile and I think this film is needed because it shows who Pinochet was and the things he did, the horrors he committed," said 28-year-old Chilean actress Paula Luchsinger, who plays a young nun in "El Conde"."And I think that this is needed so that it never happens again." (Reporting by Hanna Rantala, Editing by Rosalba O'Brien)]

Title: Actor Adam Driver takes on Netflix, Amazon over strike inaction
Text: [By Crispian BalmerVENICE, Aug 31 (Reuters) - U.S. actor Adam Driver, in Venice to promote his new film "Ferrari", criticised streaming services Netflix and Amazon on Thursday for not giving into demands by actors' and writers' unions in a strike that has hobbled the entertainment industry.The actors and writers are striking simultaneously for the first time in 63 years, demanding curbs on the use of artificial intelligence and higher pay as streaming becomes prevalent.The stoppage has prevented A-listers from promoting big studio and streamer movies at this year's Venice Film Festival in accordance with union guidance, but the stars of small independent pictures, such as "Ferrari", have been given a pass to hit the famed Lido red carpet."Why is it that a smaller distribution company like Neon, like STX International can meet the dream demands of what SAG (the Screen Actors Guild) is asking for ... but a big company like Netflix and Amazon can't?" Driver told reporters.Representatives for Netflix and Amazon did not immediately respond to a request for comment.Driver has been closely associated with Netflix in the past, representing two of their films in previous Venice festivals - "White Noise" in 2022 and "Marriage Story" in 2019.Writers have been on strike since May while actors walked off the job in July.The dual stoppages have shut down both television and movie productions in Hollywood, but some projects that have no affiliation to the big studios are receiving waivers to keep on working if they comply with the most recent union demands."Every time people from SAG go and support a movie that has agreed to these terms, the interim agreement, it just makes it more obvious that these people are willing to support the people that they collaborate with and the others are not," said Driver.Michael Mann, who directed "Ferrari", told reporters that he managed to complete the movie thanks to sacrifices made by some of the actors, producers and himself."People who worked on 'Ferrari' made it by forgoing large percentages of their salaries, in the case of Adam and myself. The producers ... basically worked for no fees," Mann said."No big studio wrote us a check. And that's why we're here, standing in solidarity with both unions." (Additional reporting by Małgorzata Wojtunik in Venice and Mary Milliken in Los Angeles; editing by Bill Berkrot)]

Title: Hollywood strikes: ‘Focus on the consumer,’ MNTN CEO says
Text: [There are several issues writers and Hollywood studios are battling over in their contract talks including streaming, AI, and writers’ rooms. Recently, media mogul Barry Diller warned of consequences for studios if they continue partnering with streaming companies like Netflix (NFLX). MNTN CEO Mark Douglas joins Yahoo Finance Live to discuss the comments.“If you look at the economics on it, I’m not sure how that quite works,” Douglas says. Douglas notes that Disney (DIS) “did about $10 billion in studio revenue last year,” whereas Netflix (NFLX) did “three times that, just by themselves. So they’re the size of like a couple of major studios combined, so I don’t know how you take an industry that seems to be largely striking over streaming and try to separate it out.”“Whenever these studios are in trouble, it’s like the finance team takes over and it just doesn’t make sense,” Douglas says. “These studios have to meet consumers where they are. The consumer sees no difference,” Douglas discusses.Douglas also notes that this is “not new. All this talk was on DVDs,” 20, 30 years ago as well. “Every time there’s a new technology, it’s like everyone’s up in arms over it. And so, bottom line, focus on the consumer, bring the content, consumers will bring the dollars, and... we can go forward with everyone entertained and the industry in a healthy state,” Douglas adds.Video Transcript- Well, key issues between Hollywood writers and studios still linger as the strike heads into its fifth month. But media mogul Barry Diller warning of catastrophic consequences should Hollywood studios continue to partner with streaming giants like Netflix, even calling it the architect of the strike on Kara Swisher's podcast. So who's poised to take on Netflix as the strike continues. Mark Douglas, MNTN CEO, joins us now. Mark, great to have you here with us in studio.MARK DOUGLAS: Yeah.- I mean, these comments are sending shockwaves right now through the equity price action of some of the largest streamers and some of them former linear powerhouses in television as well. I mean, what do you make of the comments here and could we really see some type of new negotiation process where the different studios are trying to keep Netflix out of the conversation.Story continuesMARK DOUGLAS: Well, if you look at the economics on it, I'm not sure how that quite works. So like look at Disney, for example. They did about $10 billion in studio revenue last year. Netflix is three times that just by themselves. So the size of like a couple of major studios combined. So I don't know how you take an industry that seems to be largely striking over streaming and try to separate it out, and that's like the writers and the actors that kind think that makes sense.I think the other thing you see from the comments is that whenever these studios are in trouble, it's like the finance team takes over and it just doesn't make sense. I was talking to a friend last night, I was like if we were in a restaurant, like if this restaurant had like fewer people in it, you don't call your accountant.- No.MARK DOUGLAS: You call the chef. So I think these studios have to meet consumers where they are. The consumer sees no difference. Like "Oppenheimer," three hours, I want to see it at home, I don't want to go in the theater, I'm actually willing to pay more. This is also not new. All this talk was on DVDs, you know, what, 20, 30 years ago. Every time there's a new technology, it's like everyone's up in arms over it. And so bottom line, focus on the consumer, bring the content, consumers will bring the dollars, and we can go forward with everyone entertained and the industry and the healthy state.RACHELLE AKUFFO: And Mark, Rachelle here.MARK DOUGLAS: Yeah.RACHELLE AKUFFO: As we look at Netflix, obviously holding the crown here, but then when you think of who is the next best contender, because Amazon has an interesting market there because it's usually people subscribing for Amazon not necessarily for the streaming content, it's because they've already got it for the shopping or something else. Who would be the next closest contender to a Netflix?MARK DOUGLAS: Well, I think a lot of people are thinking maybe Apple, mainly because Apple has essentially the dollars to lead a consolidation. I'm not sure that it actually makes sense for Apple because Apple's more focused on a bundle.Remember, Apple not only has Apple TV, they have Apple Music, Apple News, Apple games. And so what Apple wants is they want $20 a month from every iPhone user in the world. And they don't have to create content for music, they don't have to create content for games or for news, but they are clearly positioned, if there's going to be a consolidation, they are the ones that can lead it. Whether that makes sense for Apple as a company I'm not so sure. But they're in the best next position.I agree with you. I don't think Amazon-- that there's a lot of reasons there for Amazon to lead a consolidation of a bunch of these studios- You were talking about "Oppenheimer" a moment ago.MARK DOUGLAS: Yeah.- That's a film that was already in the can, promotion had already been done.MARK DOUGLAS: Yeah.- So by when now do many of the talks for strikes and negotiations need to be netted out by.MARK DOUGLAS: So until the actors strike, you could still film, even though the writers were on strike. And so I think when the actors went on strike, that literally has shut things down. I mean, if you look back on COVID, I mean, they went quite a while without new content and still were able to survive that. So you're looking I think Q1 and Q2 before like consumers are affected in terms of they can't get the content they want.And there are a lot of big shows out now. You have "Billions" out. You have new seasons on all these streamers. So I think the fall and the winter is taken care of. By the summer-- by the spring-- I mean, I'm sorry, by the early next year it's really going to start to affect the funnel of content that comes out and it's going to start to become a big problem.RACHELLE AKUFFO: And Mark, who do you think is most at risk in terms of losing brand loyalty. Obviously you've got consumers trying to pinch some pennies here, there might be one or two streaming services that they're going to hold on to. But then manufacturing things like live sports coming into the mix, who do you think is going to have the best brand loyalty out of the streamers.MARK DOUGLAS: Well, it's always Netflix without a doubt. The reason why is Netflix is where you go when you're not looking for your favorite show. Like I think most people I know and I'd say this for myself, when I turn on my TV, the first thing I do is see what's on Netflix. So they're positioned very well. Second thing I want is sports content, which comes from like Hulu, YouTube, TV.In the third slot, I think Disney. Everyone thought they had that locked up with Disney. Plus, but Disney has stumbled quite a bit. Their "Star Wars" content is lagging. So I think it's kind of a toss up. And a lot of people, their behavior is, well, I'll binge on Disney for three months, then I'll binge on Showtime for three months. I'll binge on Max. And so that third slot I think is the really where a lot of the competition is.The first slot, I mean, Netflix just has it on lock. They have muscle memory. Meaning you turn on your TV and you just go for Netflix. And so I think that's going to be hard for anyone to overcome.- Well, for a lot of sports fans out there, they tend to have the second spot that they go to where their team is playing. And I mean, as we're beginning NFL season. Of course, there's a different type of football that's capturing attention, there's Messi now playing in the MLS, and Apple has those rights for broadcasting and for streaming. So is the Messi effect taking hold? Is that as effective as Apple was hoping and intended it to be in this battle for some of these streaming rights for sports right now?MARK DOUGLAS: Yeah, so the way I think to always think of Apple is they don't want the fee for Apple Plus, they want the fee for the Apple bundle. So they're always going to try to put in enough content that you'll just go for the whole bundle. Basically you'll switch from Spotify to Apple Music, if you're a Spotify user.And so I think they've gone after sports, Messi made a lot of sense for them. He's like taken over-- I live in Miami. He's taken over. You see you see posters for him everywhere in Miami. So people really love that. But I don't think you'll see Apple like kind of keep going further, because their bar is to stay on track for that 19.99 a month bundle for all the services. And everyone has to remember, for three of those, they have no production costs whatsoever, right? They're just streaming music, they're not making the music. So it's particularly profitable for them.RACHELLE AKUFFO: And as a football fan, if I was going to sign up for that Apple streaming service, it would be maybe just to watch Messi play, but chances are afterwards, I probably wouldn't use the service anymore. I probably would disconnect it. But I do want to ask you, in terms of losing magic, I have to ask you about Disney Plus and how do you see their streaming strength going forward?MARK DOUGLAS: Well, I mean, they have the assets, the question is, is do they want to invest in them. I mean, they've kind of actually said they're de-emphasizing "Star Wars" a bit. Obviously they have Marvel Studios. I think Disney as a company has a lot of strength. They have all the sports I mean, if you own ESPN, I mean, to some extent you almost own sports. They have all the children's programming, family programming. And for some reason, they just seem to not be able to bundle it together in a way that they keep growing the subscribers. I think they'll figure it out. Bob Iger is obviously, a strong leader.And Disney, if you look at their revenue, it's gone up consistently over the last 10 years. Its profitability where they've stumbled. In 2019, they were doing something like $12 billion in profits, and now they're doing three, even though their revenue is higher. So I think for Disney, it's like do 10% more with 10% less. Fix the profits and just keep giving consumers what they want. That's the bottom line.- We got to go. If there's one name that you think wins out the advertising play here now with all these streaming services adding in that tier, who is it?MARK DOUGLAS: I think over the long term, it's definitely Netflix, but in the short term, I think NBC is actually a lot stronger than most people give them credit for.- All right.RACHELLE AKUFFO: All right, thanks so much. Mark Douglas there, MNTN CEO. Thank you for joining us this morning.]

Netflix had technical trouble in April when the tech behind its live Love Is Blind reunion failed—if something like that happened during the final minutes of a big game, the damage to the Netflix brand could be massive.Better than a true crime seriesWhile some sports docu-series with this all-access style have found homes on other streaming platforms—like Make or Break about professional surfers on Apple TV+—it’s noteworthy that most have ended up on Netflix.“The tennis guys were set in wanting to be with Netflix because of the reach and audience,” Martin said about producing Break Point. The idea for the show started with him and the Association of Tennis Professionals, the governing body of men’s tennis. They then brought in the Women’s Tennis Association and pitched the series to Netflix, he said.For the upcoming track and field series, the idea came from a lunch with Netflix where someone said, “Why don’t we just do the 100 meters?” according to Martin. Everyone thought it was a great idea, and Netflix brought in World Athletics, the professional association behind the sport, he said.“Everyone in the sports world understands there’s an appetite for these shows,” Martin said. It makes sense for Netflix to stay with this model rather than purchasing the rights to the sports games. Netflix isn’t in the business of creating value in something and then having to pay larger prices for rights, he said.As for the future of the genre, consumers can expect to see more streaming companies shift their budgets to produce live sports docu-series, according to Rayburn, the streaming analyst. Companies are always moving money towards what’s hot, from police procedurals to reality dating series to true crime. And right now, he said, people are talking about the style of sports documentaries Netflix has its money on.This story was originally featured on Fortune.comMore from Fortune: 5 side hustles where you may earn over $20,000 per year—all while working from homeWant more for your money? Title: Pinochet becomes a vampire in Chilean director Larrain's Venice entry 'El Conde'
Text: [By Hanna RantalaVENICE, Aug 31 (Reuters) - Chilean director Pablo Larrain, known for his Jackie Kennedy and Princess Diana dramas "Jackie" and "Spencer," chose General Augusto Pinochet as the subject of his latest film, "El Conde".The movie, which is screening in competition at the Venice Film Festival, depicts Pinochet as a 250-year-old vampire whose family gathers at his remote hideout as he decides his time on earth has come to an end.As Chile prepares to mark the 50th anniversary of the 1973 coup that brought Pinochet to power, Larrain said it was time to show him on the screen."Pinochet has never been filmed before, never been portrayed, whether in cinema or television," Larrain told a Venice press conference ahead of the Netflix title's premiere.The filmmaker, who co-wrote the movie's screenplay, chose to tell the dictator's story as a gruesome black-and-white satire."Probably it's the only way. I think that if you were to avoid the satire, it could easily take you towards some form of empathy (towards Pinochet), and that's not acceptable," said Larrain.During Pinochet's bloody 17-year dictatorship, 1,469 people were forcibly disappeared, and thousands more tortured as political prisoners, according to the Ministry of Justice, based on fact-finding by various commissions.Pinochet, who died in December 2006 at the age of 91, was never convicted of his responsibility for the crimes."There is a resurgence of the extreme right in Chile and I think this film is needed because it shows who Pinochet was and the things he did, the horrors he committed," said 28-year-old Chilean actress Paula Luchsinger, who plays a young nun in "El Conde"."And I think that this is needed so that it never happens again." (Reporting by Hanna Rantala, Editing by Rosalba O'Brien)]

Title: Hollywood strikes: ‘Focus on the consumer,’ MNTN CEO says
Text: [There are several issues writers and Hollywood studios are battling over in their contract talks including streaming, AI, and writers’ rooms. Recently, media mogul Barry Diller warned of consequences for studios if they continue partnering with streaming companies like Netflix (NFLX). MNTN CEO Mark Douglas joins Yahoo Finance Live to discuss the comments.“If you look at the economics on it, I’m not sure how that quite works,” Douglas says. Douglas notes that Disney (DIS) “did about $10 billion in studio revenue last year,” whereas Netflix (NFLX) did “three times that, just by themselves. So they’re the size of like a couple of major studios combined, so I don’t know how you take an industry that seems to be largely striking over streaming and try to separate it out.”“Whenever these studios are in trouble, it’s like the finance team takes over and it just doesn’t make sense,” Douglas says. “These studios have to meet consumers where they are. The consumer sees no difference,” Douglas discusses.Douglas also notes that this is “not new. All this talk was on DVDs,” 20, 30 years ago as well. “Every time there’s a new technology, it’s like everyone’s up in arms over it. And so, bottom line, focus on the consumer, bring the content, consumers will bring the dollars, and... we can go forward with everyone entertained and the industry in a healthy state,” Douglas adds.Video Transcript- Well, key issues between Hollywood writers and studios still linger as the strike heads into its fifth month. But media mogul Barry Diller warning of catastrophic consequences should Hollywood studios continue to partner with streaming giants like Netflix, even calling it the architect of the strike on Kara Swisher's podcast. So who's poised to take on Netflix as the strike continues. Mark Douglas, MNTN CEO, joins us now. Mark, great to have you here with us in studio.MARK DOUGLAS: Yeah.- I mean, these comments are sending shockwaves right now through the equity price action of some of the largest streamers and some of them former linear powerhouses in television as well. I mean, what do you make of the comments here and could we really see some type of new negotiation process where the different studios are trying to keep Netflix out of the conversation.Story continuesMARK DOUGLAS: Well, if you look at the economics on it, I'm not sure how that quite works. So like look at Disney, for example. They did about $10 billion in studio revenue last year. Netflix is three times that just by themselves. So the size of like a couple of major studios combined. So I don't know how you take an industry that seems to be largely striking over streaming and try to separate it out, and that's like the writers and the actors that kind think that makes sense.I think the other thing you see from the comments is that whenever these studios are in trouble, it's like the finance team takes over and it just doesn't make sense. I was talking to a friend last night, I was like if we were in a restaurant, like if this restaurant had like fewer people in it, you don't call your accountant.- No.MARK DOUGLAS: You call the chef. So I think these studios have to meet consumers where they are. The consumer sees no difference. Like "Oppenheimer," three hours, I want to see it at home, I don't want to go in the theater, I'm actually willing to pay more. This is also not new. All this talk was on DVDs, you know, what, 20, 30 years ago. Every time there's a new technology, it's like everyone's up in arms over it. And so bottom line, focus on the consumer, bring the content, consumers will bring the dollars, and we can go forward with everyone entertained and the industry and the healthy state.RACHELLE AKUFFO: And Mark, Rachelle here.MARK DOUGLAS: Yeah.RACHELLE AKUFFO: As we look at Netflix, obviously holding the crown here, but then when you think of who is the next best contender, because Amazon has an interesting market there because it's usually people subscribing for Amazon not necessarily for the streaming content, it's because they've already got it for the shopping or something else. Who would be the next closest contender to a Netflix?MARK DOUGLAS: Well, I think a lot of people are thinking maybe Apple, mainly because Apple has essentially the dollars to lead a consolidation. I'm not sure that it actually makes sense for Apple because Apple's more focused on a bundle.Remember, Apple not only has Apple TV, they have Apple Music, Apple News, Apple games. And so what Apple wants is they want $20 a month from every iPhone user in the world. And they don't have to create content for music, they don't have to create content for games or for news, but they are clearly positioned, if there's going to be a consolidation, they are the ones that can lead it. Whether that makes sense for Apple as a company I'm not so sure. But they're in the best next position.I agree with you. I don't think Amazon-- that there's a lot of reasons there for Amazon to lead a consolidation of a bunch of these studios- You were talking about "Oppenheimer" a moment ago.MARK DOUGLAS: Yeah.- That's a film that was already in the can, promotion had already been done.MARK DOUGLAS: Yeah.- So by when now do many of the talks for strikes and negotiations need to be netted out by.MARK DOUGLAS: So until the actors strike, you could still film, even though the writers were on strike. And so I think when the actors went on strike, that literally has shut things down. I mean, if you look back on COVID, I mean, they went quite a while without new content and still were able to survive that. So you're looking I think Q1 and Q2 before like consumers are affected in terms of they can't get the content they want.And there are a lot of big shows out now. You have "Billions" out. You have new seasons on all these streamers. So I think the fall and the winter is taken care of. By the summer-- by the spring-- I mean, I'm sorry, by the early next year it's really going to start to affect the funnel of content that comes out and it's going to start to become a big problem.RACHELLE AKUFFO: And Mark, who do you think is most at risk in terms of losing brand loyalty. Obviously you've got consumers trying to pinch some pennies here, there might be one or two streaming services that they're going to hold on to. But then manufacturing things like live sports coming into the mix, who do you think is going to have the best brand loyalty out of the streamers.MARK DOUGLAS: Well, it's always Netflix without a doubt. The reason why is Netflix is where you go when you're not looking for your favorite show. Like I think most people I know and I'd say this for myself, when I turn on my TV, the first thing I do is see what's on Netflix. So they're positioned very well. Second thing I want is sports content, which comes from like Hulu, YouTube, TV.In the third slot, I think Disney. Everyone thought they had that locked up with Disney. Plus, but Disney has stumbled quite a bit. Their "Star Wars" content is lagging. So I think it's kind of a toss up. And a lot of people, their behavior is, well, I'll binge on Disney for three months, then I'll binge on Showtime for three months. I'll binge on Max. And so that third slot I think is the really where a lot of the competition is.The first slot, I mean, Netflix just has it on lock. They have muscle memory. Meaning you turn on your TV and you just go for Netflix. And so I think that's going to be hard for anyone to overcome.- Well, for a lot of sports fans out there, they tend to have the second spot that they go to where their team is playing. And I mean, as we're beginning NFL season. Of course, there's a different type of football that's capturing attention, there's Messi now playing in the MLS, and Apple has those rights for broadcasting and for streaming. So is the Messi effect taking hold? Is that as effective as Apple was hoping and intended it to be in this battle for some of these streaming rights for sports right now?MARK DOUGLAS: Yeah, so the way I think to always think of Apple is they don't want the fee for Apple Plus, they want the fee for the Apple bundle. So they're always going to try to put in enough content that you'll just go for the whole bundle. Basically you'll switch from Spotify to Apple Music, if you're a Spotify user.And so I think they've gone after sports, Messi made a lot of sense for them. He's like taken over-- I live in Miami. He's taken over. You see you see posters for him everywhere in Miami. So people really love that. But I don't think you'll see Apple like kind of keep going further, because their bar is to stay on track for that 19.99 a month bundle for all the services. And everyone has to remember, for three of those, they have no production costs whatsoever, right? They're just streaming music, they're not making the music. So it's particularly profitable for them.RACHELLE AKUFFO: And as a football fan, if I was going to sign up for that Apple streaming service, it would be maybe just to watch Messi play, but chances are afterwards, I probably wouldn't use the service anymore. I probably would disconnect it. But I do want to ask you, in terms of losing magic, I have to ask you about Disney Plus and how do you see their streaming strength going forward?MARK DOUGLAS: Well, I mean, they have the assets, the question is, is do they want to invest in them. I mean, they've kind of actually said they're de-emphasizing "Star Wars" a bit. Obviously they have Marvel Studios. I think Disney as a company has a lot of strength. They have all the sports I mean, if you own ESPN, I mean, to some extent you almost own sports. They have all the children's programming, family programming. And for some reason, they just seem to not be able to bundle it together in a way that they keep growing the subscribers. I think they'll figure it out. Bob Iger is obviously, a strong leader.And Disney, if you look at their revenue, it's gone up consistently over the last 10 years. Its profitability where they've stumbled. In 2019, they were doing something like $12 billion in profits, and now they're doing three, even though their revenue is higher. So I think for Disney, it's like do 10% more with 10% less. Fix the profits and just keep giving consumers what they want. That's the bottom line.- We got to go. If there's one name that you think wins out the advertising play here now with all these streaming services adding in that tier, who is it?MARK DOUGLAS: I think over the long term, it's definitely Netflix, but in the short term, I think NBC is actually a lot stronger than most people give them credit for.- All right.RACHELLE AKUFFO: All right, thanks so much. Mark Douglas there, MNTN CEO. Thank you for joining us this morning.]

Title: Disney vs. Charter: Cable companies may feel 'emboldened,' analyst says
Text: [If you are a customer of Charter's Spectrum (CHTR), you won't be finding Disney-owned channels (DIS) in your cable lineup. Disney pulled its channels from Spectrum amid a carriage dispute between the two companies. Goldman Sachs Managing Director Brett Feldman says there are two reasons why this dispute is happening.First with the decline in cable subscribers is accelerating, falling about 6% to 7% this year. Feldman says that's interesting because, historically, media companies have been able to raise the prices of their channels by about 5% to 6% a year. "We've hit this tipping point now where the media companies simply can't raise prices fast enough to offset the loss of paid TV subscribers," Feldman says, going on to say that it has "emboldened" cable companies to start discussing the possibility of a new model.The second thing is that the cable companies have reached the "point of economic indifference," Feldman says. What that means is that given how much cord-cutting is happening, Charter is losing so much profitability in that business and "basically what they're saying is we almost don't care anymore whether our customers decide to pay for a channel package or not," Feldman says, adding that they are primarily making their money by providing internet service.Click here for more of Yahoo Finance's coverage from the Goldman Sachs Communacopia tech conference.Video Transcript[AUDIO LOGO]BRIAN SOZZI: Welcome back to "Yahoo Finance Live." We're still live at the Goldman Sachs Tech and Media Conference in San Francisco. And the other undercurrent at this conference is in fact all things happening in media. Lots of focus, of course, on AI. But that undercurrent is media and what might be happening next.And to that end, Brett Feldman is here, Goldman Sachs Managing Director covering telecom, cable, and media. Thanks for having us to your conference, Brett. We appreciate it.BRETT FELDMAN: We're so excited to have you here. This is one of the biggest events we do all year. We're going to have the senior leaders and CEOs from over 200 global TMT companies that really should be a great couple of days.Story continuesBRIAN SOZZI: No, it's already shaping up to be that way. And a lot of the chatter in the room is the situation between Charter and Disney. And my question to you is, why is this happening right now?BRETT FELDMAN: That's right. So just for your viewers, who I think probably know by this point in time, if you're a Charter customer, so if you have spectrum cable, you can't get any Disney channels right now. They've been removed from the service. And that includes ESPN.So you made a great point. We've been seeing the number of households that pay for cable and satellite TV bundles decline for years. Why are we now just getting to this point where the distributors, the cable companies are really pushing back? There's really two reasons why. The first is we're going to see the total number of households that pay for TV this year decline by about 6% to 7%. About two years ago, that was negative 5%. A couple of years before that, it was a much more moderate number. So this has been an accelerating pace of decline.The reason why 6% to 7% is interesting is that historically, the media companies, companies like Disney, have been able to raise the price of their channels by about 5% to 6% per year. So we've hit this tipping point now where the media companies simply can't raise prices fast enough to offset the loss of paid TV subscribers. I think that has emboldened the cable companies to look at this relationship and say, listen, we can't absorb these historical price increases. We need to talk about a new model. That's one of the things that Charter talked about.Another point Charter made is the point we actually started making about four years ago, which is that they've reached what they call a point of economic indifference. Basically, they're saying we almost don't care anymore, whether our customers decide to pay for a channel package or not, because they've lost so much profitability in that business as a result of cord cutting. They really make all their money now providing internet service.And so I think that you have the cable companies saying, we can't do this anymore. We were able to deal with it for a couple of years when we were losing a small number of customers. But as this snowball continues to roll down the hill, we have to come up with a new model.BRIAN SOZZI: At the end of the day, when this comes to an end, and it inevitably will, who is the biggest loser? And what does it mean to the broader media landscape?BRETT FELDMAN: It's a great question. And actually, we're going to be asking a version of that question to all these CEOs of the big media and cable companies when they're here this week. And really, the question we're going to be trying to get an answer to is, what's a win-win?If the model that we've had before, the relationship between the media companies, between the cable and satellite companies, and the relationship that they ultimately have with their viewers, if that's not working anymore, what is going to work? And are there other things that have to change? Maybe the way they price their streaming services in order to get something that works for everyone involved, including the consumer.BRIAN SOZZI: Do you agree-- I think it was last week, Barry Diller at IAC said the streaming companies, they're not your friends. They're your enemies is the ultimate problem here companies like a Netflix.BRETT FELDMAN: I think Charter has been trying to make that point. Their view is that the media companies have devalued their entertainment by moving on to streaming platforms. And they give examples of it. They say, historically, you've been able to capture some of that value through advertising. You're barely doing any advertising on your streaming platforms. It's a new thing, and you're not doing a lot of it.There's no security. It used to be that if you wanted to watch what was on cable TV, you had to pay for cable TV in your home. I think we all know that password sharing has become a big deal. Netflix has recently started cracking down on that, but not all of the media companies have. And just in general, I think that the distributors, the cable and satellite companies, they look at what they're being asked to pay to make that content available to their customers. And they look at the price that those same media companies are charging to make it available on a direct basis. They say these are not the same prices. There's got to be a way that we come up with a sustainable economic model we can all agree on.BRIAN SOZZI: Is there any appetite to own these media stocks, and what has to happen?BRETT FELDMAN: Well, I think there is, in part, because they've been under so much pressure. A stock that we have talked a lot about is Warner Brothers Discovery, David Zaslav, the CEO of Warner Brothers--BRIAN SOZZI: He will be here.BRETT FELDMAN: --will be here tomorrow. They are able to do something that some of the other media companies cannot, which is that they're still integrating a very large merger. They had acquired the Time Warner assets, the old Time Warner assets out of AT&T about two years ago. And they quickly realized that there was a lot of inefficiency in how that business was run. And so they have an opportunity here to keep taking costs out of the business. And hopefully make the products better at the same time, so that they can generate cash, they can pay down debt, and ultimately do something that should be accretive to their shareholders by positioning the company to be a winner in the streaming wars.But to be fair, it's a highly debated sector, that's a highly debated stock.BRIAN SOZZI: Not lost on me, Brett, is last year, Bob Chapek was here, now former CEO of Disney. Disney CEO Bob Iger is not here. Of course, there's always scheduling conflicts, et cetera, et cetera. But to me, I think it says a lot that Disney is not at this premier conference. And it says a lot about the challenges they're going through. What has to happen to get investor appetite back into a stock that's about 52-week lows, despite the content power that is Disney?BRETT FELDMAN: Well, Disney has been here for a number of years. And so it would have been great if we could have made the scheduling work. But we'll hopefully, we'll have Bob Iger back.There's a few things they have to do. They have to demonstrate that they can continue to be on a path to profitability in streaming. So one of the nice inflections that we've seen since Bob Iger returned is that the losses they've been incurring in their streaming business have begun to compress very significantly. So proving that they can make money and then give some indication as to what those margins can be over time, I think that's really important.I think in their traditional media networks business, which is really revolves around ESPN, they have to show that they can transition ESPN from being a package of cable and satellite TV channels to being something that you can subscribe to on a direct basis, meaning something you could stream. A lot of people may say, well, hold on, can't you get ESPN Plus right now, you get that in your bundle with Disney Plus? It's not the same thing. It's a niche product they haven't put the full suite of sports rights that they have access to into that product.If they can do those two things, they will really be able to demonstrate that they have a strategy and a model for taking what is a very profitable, historically, very profitable media business, and turning it into a profitable streaming media business.BRIAN SOZZI: And Bob made a lot of headlines a couple of months ago, suggesting everything was on the table. What's the end game here for him? Is it a spinoff of ESPN? Is it a sale of those linear TV assets?BRETT FELDMAN: I don't think we know. I thought what was refreshing about those comments-- I think some people heard them as a little bit alarming. But I think that what was refreshing was to hear him acknowledge that everything is on the table.You know, if you go back a few years when cord-cutting wasn't quite as intense as it is right now. In some cases, you would hear media companies talk about this being manageable, taking a very long time, not likely to get any worse. I think investors were always very skeptical of that. To hear a leader in the industry like Bob Iger acknowledge that you have to put everything on the table right now, I think, shows how seriously they're taking this and is a real signal to the Street that they are going to do what they need to do, so that Disney can have another 100 years of success in the market.BRIAN SOZZI: Are investors waiting for that big move to get back into the stock? Do they want to see him pull the trigger on something mind-blowing?BRETT FELDMAN: I don't know if it's one thing. I think you have to look at this and say, as he's returned to the company, he has made the adjustments that are necessary to put the company on the path they need to be on, because what investors really want is they want to see a company that can execute its way to success. And if you're still debating what they're supposed to do, that can be an overhang on the stock. So the main thing is setting a strategy and then setting a strategy that the market thinks will work if you execute it.BRIAN SOZZI: Along the lines of Disney hit a 52-week low, I look at Paramount. You still rate the stock a sell, right? What has to happen to get investors excited about that name?BRETT FELDMAN: You know, Paramount faces a lot of the same issues that Disney faces a lot of the same issues that Warner Brothers Discovery faces. One of the things that they are very committed to is continuing to invest in their streaming platform. So whereas many of the other media companies have already moved past peak investment, meaning that they're getting closer to breaking even not farther away, this year Paramount will probably see their peak losses, meaning they're still leaning into the investment.To their credit, the service has been much more popular with viewers. And I think a lot of people guessed. And they've had some real hits. They've put the NFL on the platform. So I think they feel very good about the subscriber momentum, what they have to be able to demonstrate to investors is that they can not only pivot away from being an investment phase but accelerate towards making money in their streaming business, because they, just like everyone else, are going to see their legacy networks come under increasing pressure.BRIAN SOZZI: Brett Feldman, Goldman Sachs Managing Director covering telecom, cable, and media. Thank you for having us at your conference. This is one of our favorite ones by far.BRETT FELDMAN: Thanks for being here.]

Title: Aaron Paul says he doesn’t earn a penny from ‘Breaking Bad’ streaming on Netflix despite the show’s ongoing popularity
Text: [Aaron Paul, one of the stars of Breaking Bad, says despite the show’s ongoing popularity on Netflix, he does not see any residual payments from those streams.While walking the picket line in the ongoing SAG-AFTRA strike against studios and streaming services, Paul revealed the news, saying he believes the time has come for Netflix to pay talent appropriately."I don't get a piece from Netflix on Breaking Bad to be totally honest and that's insane to me,” he said. “Shows live forever on these streamers and they live forever. … I think a lot of these streamers know that they have been getting away with not paying people a fair wage and now it's time to pony up."Aaron Paul revealed that he earns $0 in residuals from streaming despite BREAKING BAD doing constant numbers for streamers. "I don't get a piece from Netflix on BREAKING BAD to be totally honest and that's insane to me." #AMPTP pic.twitter.com/iqiz2yVy50— Todd Spence (@Todd_Spence) September 4, 2023The fact that one of the stars of arguably one of the biggest shows on television in the past decade (and certainly one of the buzziest) is not getting paid from its continued streaming raised questions about who, exactly, is benefiting from it financially.Ten years ago, Breaking Bad was the most popular show on Netflix and, while it has fallen out of the Top 10, per the company, it’s still incredibly popular with viewers. Ironically, Netflix can be credited, in part, with boosting the show’s overall popularity by bringing it on its streaming platform while the show was still airing on AMC, its original network.After the drama began airing, the show's popularity on AMC grew over time, the opposite of the falloff in viewers that shows typically experience. The season four finale attracted fewer than 2 million viewers. The series finale, two years later, had 10 million people watching.Story continues(In fairness, AMC would also run marathons of the show, which could have helped boost viewership as well.)While Paul took Netflix to task for the lack of payments, he and his Breaking Bad cast members did reunite recently to urge Hollywood studios to resume negotiations with striking actors. Warner Bros. Discovery, on Monday, adjusted its earnings forecast, saying it assumed the financial impact of the strikes will persist through at least the end of the year.Netflix, meanwhile, will stop streaming Breaking Bad in February 2025.This story was originally featured on Fortune.comMore from Fortune: 5 side hustles where you may earn over $20,000 per year—all while working from homeWant more for your money? Title: Netflix the 'most frequently' canceled streaming service, survey finds
Text: [Americans cutting back on their streaming subscriptions are turning to Netflix (NFLX) first, according to a new survey.The survey from Vorhaus Advisors, which included responses from 2,000 people in the US over 18, found that among those who canceled a streaming service in the past three months, Netflix was the "most frequently mentioned" service, followed by Disney's Hulu (DIS) and Amazon Prime (AMZN).The survey findings come at an inflection point for media, and Netflix is particularly in the crosshairs as it has sought to jumpstart subscriber growth in recent months and years through a crackdown on password-sharing. "When you're the biggest, you're going to be hit really hard with cancellations," Vorhaus Advisors CEO Mike Vorhaus said on Tuesday at the Goldman Sachs Communacopia and Tech Conference in San Francisco. "The problem for them in the United States is that everybody who has conflicts today, plus everybody who has ever had to cancel, adds up pretty much to the total number of people that would consider ever joining a streaming service. They've already said no to Netflix once, so now there's that contest to get them back and that's quite a struggle."Though Netflix has its challenges, there's more than enough cord-cutting to go around right now. The data shows that 12% of paid TV subscribers are "very likely to cut the cord in the next year," and those who are most likely to do so are between the ages of 18 and 34.About 47% of people who cancel services do so to save money.Netflix logo on a TV screen in Poland on Nov. 29, 2020. (Jakub Porzycki/NurPhoto via Getty Images) (NurPhoto via Getty Images)Still, for traditional TV outlets, digital video is creating additional pressure. Every day, 2 out of 5 Americans watch videos on the internet, the Vorhaus survey revealed. Across all age categories, there are increases in daily digital video viewing between 7% and 10%.In part, what's opening the door to this kind of transition is a change in storytelling, Vorhaus told the audience.Story continues"The idea that a story has to be scripted, that the story has to have big actors in it, that the story must have a budget, and a beginning, middle, and end — the world has changed," he said."With all due respect, the story isn't 'When Harry Met Sally' anymore," Vorhaus added. "I remember when people in Hollywood were saying that 'The Matrix' wasn't a story. So I think the people who make money will be the ones who are able to figure out what storytelling means."Read more coverage of the 2023 Goldman Sachs Communacopia + Tech conference:CrowdStrike CEO: 'Microsoft is always going to be a competitor'Visa CEO: Consumer spending showing 'stability, resiliency'The AI market will be worth $600 billion, Nvidia exec saysGoldman Sachs chief economist: US consumer won't break in 2024Potential FTC antitrust suit against Amazon may hang over the stock: AnalystDisney must show turnaround success for its stock to rise from the ashes: AnalystDisney and Comcast move up Hulu deal date to Sept. 30Allie Garfinkle is a Senior Tech Reporter at Yahoo Finance. Title: Netflix co-CEO: Dealmaking isn't off the table, but we'll be 'very choosy'
Text: [Netflix (NFLX) is looking for growth, and it will do what it needs to do to get it, Netflix co-CEO Greg Peters said Tuesday at the Goldman Sachs Communacopia and Tech Conference in San Francisco."Our top priority is to fuel the growth of the business by focusing on the core that we've been focused on for so long," Peters told the audience. "A second-order component for this is when we very selectively find M&A opportunities that we think meet all of our criteria."Peters, who joined Ted Sarandos in the dual CEO role earlier this year, said that moving forward Netflix will be more exacting about M&A."We've been very, very choosy about [deals] because we think that there's a lot of opportunity," Peters added. "It's very complicated versus focusing on the core."Greg Peters, co-CEO of Netflix, during a keynote about the future of entertainment on the second day of the Mobile World Congress 2023 on Feb. 28, 2023, in Barcelona, Spain. (Joan Cros/NurPhoto via Getty Images) (NurPhoto via Getty Images)The company is reportedly eyeing intellectual property deals and could be considering acquiring traditional Hollywood assets, such as studios.In the past, Netflix has acquired studios such as Australian animation studio Animal Logic and made intellectual property deals such as its 2021 acquisition of the Roald Dahl Story Company. The streaming company has also scooped up gaming studios in recent years.However, looking ahead, content will be the key investment that Peters sees Netflix doubling down on."The biggest thing is if we can actually execute against the investments that we're making already," Peters said. "That's the highest-leverage, most impactful thing you can do with what our users care about the most, and so we're putting most of our energy and attention on making that better."Netflix has kept a close eye on profitability this year as it executes against those investments by doubling down on cost-cutting, cracking down on password-sharing, and finding ways to save on original content, as Yahoo Finance's Allie Canal previously reported.It's all part of a strategy of "wanting to take fewer swings but better swings," Third Bridge analyst Jamie Lumley told Yahoo Finance in June.Story continuesDespite a backdrop of a historic Hollywood strike and the mounting costs that come with that — which moderators didn't ask Peters about — Netflix's efforts appear to be paying off so far.Netflix stock has risen north of 50% year to date and over 100% over the last 12 months.Read more coverage of the 2023 Goldman Sachs Communacopia + Tech conference:CrowdStrike CEO: 'Microsoft is always going to be a competitor'Visa CEO: Consumer spending showing 'stability, resiliency'The AI market will be worth $600 billion, Nvidia exec saysGoldman Sachs chief economist: US consumer won't break in 2024Potential FTC antitrust suit against Amazon may hang over the stock: AnalystDisney must show turnaround success for its stock to rise from the ashes: AnalystDisney and Comcast move up Hulu deal date to Sept. 30-Allie Garfinkle is a Senior Tech Reporter at Yahoo Finance. Title: Disney vs. Charter: Cable companies may feel 'emboldened,' analyst says
Text: [If you are a customer of Charter's Spectrum (CHTR), you won't be finding Disney-owned channels (DIS) in your cable lineup. Disney pulled its channels from Spectrum amid a carriage dispute between the two companies. Goldman Sachs Managing Director Brett Feldman says there are two reasons why this dispute is happening.First with the decline in cable subscribers is accelerating, falling about 6% to 7% this year. Feldman says that's interesting because, historically, media companies have been able to raise the prices of their channels by about 5% to 6% a year. "We've hit this tipping point now where the media companies simply can't raise prices fast enough to offset the loss of paid TV subscribers," Feldman says, going on to say that it has "emboldened" cable companies to start discussing the possibility of a new model.The second thing is that the cable companies have reached the "point of economic indifference," Feldman says. What that means is that given how much cord-cutting is happening, Charter is losing so much profitability in that business and "basically what they're saying is we almost don't care anymore whether our customers decide to pay for a channel package or not," Feldman says, adding that they are primarily making their money by providing internet service.Click here for more of Yahoo Finance's coverage from the Goldman Sachs Communacopia tech conference.Video Transcript[AUDIO LOGO]BRIAN SOZZI: Welcome back to "Yahoo Finance Live." We're still live at the Goldman Sachs Tech and Media Conference in San Francisco. And the other undercurrent at this conference is in fact all things happening in media. Lots of focus, of course, on AI. But that undercurrent is media and what might be happening next.And to that end, Brett Feldman is here, Goldman Sachs Managing Director covering telecom, cable, and media. Thanks for having us to your conference, Brett. We appreciate it.BRETT FELDMAN: We're so excited to have you here. This is one of the biggest events we do all year. We're going to have the senior leaders and CEOs from over 200 global TMT companies that really should be a great couple of days.Story continuesBRIAN SOZZI: No, it's already shaping up to be that way. And a lot of the chatter in the room is the situation between Charter and Disney. And my question to you is, why is this happening right now?BRETT FELDMAN: That's right. So just for your viewers, who I think probably know by this point in time, if you're a Charter customer, so if you have spectrum cable, you can't get any Disney channels right now. They've been removed from the service. And that includes ESPN.So you made a great point. We've been seeing the number of households that pay for cable and satellite TV bundles decline for years. Why are we now just getting to this point where the distributors, the cable companies are really pushing back? There's really two reasons why. The first is we're going to see the total number of households that pay for TV this year decline by about 6% to 7%. About two years ago, that was negative 5%. A couple of years before that, it was a much more moderate number. So this has been an accelerating pace of decline.The reason why 6% to 7% is interesting is that historically, the media companies, companies like Disney, have been able to raise the price of their channels by about 5% to 6% per year. So we've hit this tipping point now where the media companies simply can't raise prices fast enough to offset the loss of paid TV subscribers. I think that has emboldened the cable companies to look at this relationship and say, listen, we can't absorb these historical price increases. We need to talk about a new model. That's one of the things that Charter talked about.Another point Charter made is the point we actually started making about four years ago, which is that they've reached what they call a point of economic indifference. Basically, they're saying we almost don't care anymore, whether our customers decide to pay for a channel package or not, because they've lost so much profitability in that business as a result of cord cutting. They really make all their money now providing internet service.And so I think that you have the cable companies saying, we can't do this anymore. We were able to deal with it for a couple of years when we were losing a small number of customers. But as this snowball continues to roll down the hill, we have to come up with a new model.BRIAN SOZZI: At the end of the day, when this comes to an end, and it inevitably will, who is the biggest loser? And what does it mean to the broader media landscape?BRETT FELDMAN: It's a great question. And actually, we're going to be asking a version of that question to all these CEOs of the big media and cable companies when they're here this week. And really, the question we're going to be trying to get an answer to is, what's a win-win?If the model that we've had before, the relationship between the media companies, between the cable and satellite companies, and the relationship that they ultimately have with their viewers, if that's not working anymore, what is going to work? And are there other things that have to change? Maybe the way they price their streaming services in order to get something that works for everyone involved, including the consumer.BRIAN SOZZI: Do you agree-- I think it was last week, Barry Diller at IAC said the streaming companies, they're not your friends. They're your enemies is the ultimate problem here companies like a Netflix.BRETT FELDMAN: I think Charter has been trying to make that point. Their view is that the media companies have devalued their entertainment by moving on to streaming platforms. And they give examples of it. They say, historically, you've been able to capture some of that value through advertising. You're barely doing any advertising on your streaming platforms. It's a new thing, and you're not doing a lot of it.There's no security. It used to be that if you wanted to watch what was on cable TV, you had to pay for cable TV in your home. I think we all know that password sharing has become a big deal. Netflix has recently started cracking down on that, but not all of the media companies have. And just in general, I think that the distributors, the cable and satellite companies, they look at what they're being asked to pay to make that content available to their customers. And they look at the price that those same media companies are charging to make it available on a direct basis. They say these are not the same prices. There's got to be a way that we come up with a sustainable economic model we can all agree on.BRIAN SOZZI: Is there any appetite to own these media stocks, and what has to happen?BRETT FELDMAN: Well, I think there is, in part, because they've been under so much pressure. A stock that we have talked a lot about is Warner Brothers Discovery, David Zaslav, the CEO of Warner Brothers--BRIAN SOZZI: He will be here.BRETT FELDMAN: --will be here tomorrow. They are able to do something that some of the other media companies cannot, which is that they're still integrating a very large merger. They had acquired the Time Warner assets, the old Time Warner assets out of AT&T about two years ago. And they quickly realized that there was a lot of inefficiency in how that business was run. And so they have an opportunity here to keep taking costs out of the business. And hopefully make the products better at the same time, so that they can generate cash, they can pay down debt, and ultimately do something that should be accretive to their shareholders by positioning the company to be a winner in the streaming wars.But to be fair, it's a highly debated sector, that's a highly debated stock.BRIAN SOZZI: Not lost on me, Brett, is last year, Bob Chapek was here, now former CEO of Disney. Disney CEO Bob Iger is not here. Of course, there's always scheduling conflicts, et cetera, et cetera. But to me, I think it says a lot that Disney is not at this premier conference. And it says a lot about the challenges they're going through. What has to happen to get investor appetite back into a stock that's about 52-week lows, despite the content power that is Disney?BRETT FELDMAN: Well, Disney has been here for a number of years. And so it would have been great if we could have made the scheduling work. But we'll hopefully, we'll have Bob Iger back.There's a few things they have to do. They have to demonstrate that they can continue to be on a path to profitability in streaming. So one of the nice inflections that we've seen since Bob Iger returned is that the losses they've been incurring in their streaming business have begun to compress very significantly. So proving that they can make money and then give some indication as to what those margins can be over time, I think that's really important.I think in their traditional media networks business, which is really revolves around ESPN, they have to show that they can transition ESPN from being a package of cable and satellite TV channels to being something that you can subscribe to on a direct basis, meaning something you could stream. A lot of people may say, well, hold on, can't you get ESPN Plus right now, you get that in your bundle with Disney Plus? It's not the same thing. It's a niche product they haven't put the full suite of sports rights that they have access to into that product.If they can do those two things, they will really be able to demonstrate that they have a strategy and a model for taking what is a very profitable, historically, very profitable media business, and turning it into a profitable streaming media business.BRIAN SOZZI: And Bob made a lot of headlines a couple of months ago, suggesting everything was on the table. What's the end game here for him? Is it a spinoff of ESPN? Is it a sale of those linear TV assets?BRETT FELDMAN: I don't think we know. I thought what was refreshing about those comments-- I think some people heard them as a little bit alarming. But I think that what was refreshing was to hear him acknowledge that everything is on the table.You know, if you go back a few years when cord-cutting wasn't quite as intense as it is right now. In some cases, you would hear media companies talk about this being manageable, taking a very long time, not likely to get any worse. I think investors were always very skeptical of that. To hear a leader in the industry like Bob Iger acknowledge that you have to put everything on the table right now, I think, shows how seriously they're taking this and is a real signal to the Street that they are going to do what they need to do, so that Disney can have another 100 years of success in the market.BRIAN SOZZI: Are investors waiting for that big move to get back into the stock? Do they want to see him pull the trigger on something mind-blowing?BRETT FELDMAN: I don't know if it's one thing. I think you have to look at this and say, as he's returned to the company, he has made the adjustments that are necessary to put the company on the path they need to be on, because what investors really want is they want to see a company that can execute its way to success. And if you're still debating what they're supposed to do, that can be an overhang on the stock. So the main thing is setting a strategy and then setting a strategy that the market thinks will work if you execute it.BRIAN SOZZI: Along the lines of Disney hit a 52-week low, I look at Paramount. You still rate the stock a sell, right? What has to happen to get investors excited about that name?BRETT FELDMAN: You know, Paramount faces a lot of the same issues that Disney faces a lot of the same issues that Warner Brothers Discovery faces. One of the things that they are very committed to is continuing to invest in their streaming platform. So whereas many of the other media companies have already moved past peak investment, meaning that they're getting closer to breaking even not farther away, this year Paramount will probably see their peak losses, meaning they're still leaning into the investment.To their credit, the service has been much more popular with viewers. And I think a lot of people guessed. And they've had some real hits. They've put the NFL on the platform. So I think they feel very good about the subscriber momentum, what they have to be able to demonstrate to investors is that they can not only pivot away from being an investment phase but accelerate towards making money in their streaming business, because they, just like everyone else, are going to see their legacy networks come under increasing pressure.BRIAN SOZZI: Brett Feldman, Goldman Sachs Managing Director covering telecom, cable, and media. Thank you for having us at your conference. This is one of our favorite ones by far.BRETT FELDMAN: Thanks for being here.]
